Force GPU memory cleanup

Source: R/gpu-memory.R
gpu_gc.Rd

Triggers R garbage collection to free GPU memory held by unreferenced tbl_gpu objects. Use this between operations when GPU memory is limited or before large allocations.

Usage

gpu_gc(verbose = FALSE, aggressive = TRUE)

Arguments

verbose

Logical. If TRUE, prints memory freed. Default FALSE.

aggressive

Logical. If TRUE (default), runs multiple GC passes with short delays to more aggressively trigger finalizers. If FALSE, runs a lighter cleanup pass.

Value

Invisibly returns a list with memory state before and after cleanup, and the amount freed in bytes and gigabytes. freed_bytes is the drop in pool_used_bytes (allocator level) when cuplyr's memory resource is installed, since the device-level free memory does not move while the resource keeps its pages; with resource == "cuda" it is the rise in device free memory. released_bytes is what the resource gave back to the device: the drop in pool_bytes across the call. Under "async" the call ends by trimming the async pool, so it is the memory the pool held unused (0 or more); under "pool" it is 0 (RMM's pool never shrinks); under "cuda" it is NA.

Details

GPU memory is automatically freed when tbl_gpu objects are garbage collected by R. However, R's garbage collector doesn't know about GPU memory pressure and may not run immediately. This function forces garbage collection and allows time for GPU cleanup.

A cuplyr call you make (an eager verb, compute(), collect(), a bind) frees the temporary GPU tables its own steps built when it returns. What a call returns is yours and is never freed early, including a table that your code creates while a verb evaluates its arguments or expressions. So this function is for tables you created and dropped without R having collected them yet: the group_by() result of a one-line pipeline lives until R's next collection. So does the inner result of a dplyr verb that dplyr itself builds from several verb calls, such as add_tally(sort = TRUE). When a GPU step runs out of device memory, cuplyr runs gc() and gpu_gc(aggressive = FALSE) itself and retries that step once; a second failure raises an error of class cuplyr_error_gpu_oom.

Under the default "async" resource, this function also synchronises the device and returns all unused memory of cuplyr's async pool to the device, so other processes can use it (see gpu_memory_state() and vignette("memory", package = "cuplyr")). The pool is then smaller than the session's recent peak, so the next calls grow it again from the driver; that costs the first call after gpu_gc() a few percent. If the device is in a CUDA error state, the return step cannot run: gpu_gc() then gives a warning instead of an error and leaves the pool as it is, so it stays safe in cleanup code.

Call this function:

  • After removing large GPU objects with rm(), when other processes need the memory (under "async" it returns what the pool holds unused)

  • When you see out-of-memory errors

  • Before allocating large new GPU tables

It is not meant for the loop of a benchmark: under "async" the trim makes the next call grow the pool again.

See also

gpu_memory_state for checking current memory usage

Examples

if (has_gpu()) {
  # Create and discard a GPU table
  gpu_df <- tbl_gpu(data.frame(x = runif(1000000)))
  rm(gpu_df)

  # Force cleanup
  gpu_gc(verbose = TRUE)
}
#> GPU memory freed: 8002816 bytes (allocator level)
#> Returned to the device: 1.04 GB
